items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles"?
items.answer: Golgi apparatus
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Golgi apparatus.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Prokaryotes are inefficient because they lack a nucleus." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Prokaryotes are highly successful; without a nucleus they can transcribe and translate simultaneously and respond rapidly, though they cannot process mRNA in the same way.
items.markingKey: Prokaryotes are highly successful; without a nucleus they can transcribe and translate simultaneously and respond rapidly, though they cannot process mRNA in the same way. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between ribosomes bound to rough ER and free ribosomes.
items.answer: Free ribosomes make proteins used within the cytoplasm; ribosomes on rough ER make proteins that enter the ER for secretion, insertion in membranes or delivery to lysosomes.
items.markingKey: Free ribosomes make proteins used within the cytoplasm; ribosomes on rough ER make proteins that enter the ER for secretion, insertion in membranes or delivery to lysosomes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cell is treated with a drug that blocks nuclear pores. Which process is most directly affected?
options: export of mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm
diffusion of O₂ into the cell
items.answer: export of mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm
items.markingKey: B. mRNA leaves via pores.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Tay–Sachs disease shows the role of lysosomes.
items.answer: A missing lysosomal enzyme (hexosaminidase A) causes lipids to accumulate in neurones. Lysosomes contain specific hydrolases; if one is absent, its substrate builds up and damages cells.
items.markingKey: Context (A missing lysosomal enzyme (hexosaminidase A) causes lipids to accumulate in neurones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lysosomes contain specific hydrolases; if one is absent, its substrate builds up and damages cells. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of lysosomes.

items.stem:
Cubes of agar containing phenolphthalein (pink in alkali) were placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The time taken for each cube to become completely colourless was recorded.

Side length / cm | SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹ | Time to decolourise / min
0.5 | 12.0 | 0.1
1.0 | ? | 0.2
1.5 | 4.0 | 0.3
2.0 | 3.0 | 0.3
2.5 | 2.4 | 0.5

(a) Calculate the SA:V ratio of the 1.0 cm cube. [2]
(b) Describe the relationship between SA:V ratio and the time taken to decolourise. [1]
(c) Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of acid into the 2.5 cm cube in cm per minute. [2]
items.answer: (a) 6.0 cm⁻¹ (b) As SA:V ratio decreases (larger cubes), time increases. (c) 2.500 cm min⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) [2] SA = 6 × 1.0² = 6.00; V = 1.000 (M1); ratio 6.0 (A1). (b) [1] Inverse relationship described (A1). (c) [2] Distance to centre = 1.25 cm (M1); 1.25/0.5 = 2.500 cm min⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Which structure is not usually considered an organelle because it is not a discrete subunit?
items.answer: the cytoplasm
items.markingKey: B. The cytoskeleton, cell wall and cytoplasm are not counted as organelles.

items.stem: Why is the homogenate in cell fractionation kept ice-cold, isotonic and buffered?
options: To reduce enzyme activity, prevent osmotic damage to organelles and prevent denaturation by pH changes.
items.answer: To reduce enzyme activity, prevent osmotic damage to organelles and prevent denaturation by pH changes.
items.markingKey: C. Each condition protects organelles.

items.stem: Explain the advantages of compartmentalisation in eukaryotic cells.
items.answer: Enzymes and substrates can be concentrated in a small volume; incompatible reactions or conditions (e.g. low pH in lysosomes) are separated; damaging substances are isolated; membranes provide surfaces for enzymes and gradients (e.g. in mitochondria).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Enzymes and substrates can be concentrated in a small volume; incompatible reactions or conditions (e.g. low pH in lysosomes) are separated; damaging substances are isolated; membranes provide surfaces for enzymes and gradients (e.g. in mitochondria). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Amara writes: "The Golgi apparatus makes proteins." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Proteins are made on ribosomes; the Golgi modifies (e.g. glycosylates), sorts and packages them.
items.markingKey: Proteins are made on ribosomes; the Golgi modifies (e.g. glycosylates), sorts and packages them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Cubes of agar containing phenolphthalein (pink in alkali) were placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The time taken for each cube to become completely colourless was recorded.

Side length / cm | SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹ | Time to decolourise / min
0.5 | 12.0 | 0.1
1.0 | 6.0 | 0.1
1.5 | ? | 0.2
2.0 | 3.0 | 0.3
2.5 | 2.4 | 0.4

(a) Calculate the SA:V ratio of the 1.5 cm cube. [2]
(b) Describe the relationship between SA:V ratio and the time taken to decolourise. [1]
(c) Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of acid into the 2.5 cm cube in cm per minute. [2]
items.answer: (a) 4.0 cm⁻¹ (b) As SA:V ratio decreases (larger cubes), time increases. (c) 3.125 cm min⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) [2] SA = 6 × 1.5² = 13.50; V = 3.375 (M1); ratio 4.0 (A1). (b) [1] Inverse relationship described (A1). (c) [2] Distance to centre = 1.25 cm (M1); 1.25/0.4 = 3.125 cm min⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Compartmentalisation explains the success of eukaryotic cells."
items.answer: Compartmentalisation enabled eukaryotic complexity, but “success” can also be measured by abundance and diversity, where prokaryotes excel.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it allows larger cells with specialised, efficient internal environments; it underpins multicellularity and complex regulation. Arguments against: prokaryotes are more numerous and metabolically diverse, and thrive without it; compartments add energy costs for transport between them. Supported judgement: Compartmentalisation enabled eukaryotic complexity, but “success” can also be measured by abundance and diversity, where prokaryotes excel. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Where in the mitochondrion is the electron transport chain located?
items.answer: on the inner membrane (cristae)
items.markingKey: A. Proteins of the ETC and ATP synthase are embedded in cristae.

items.stem: Why do cells with high energy demands, such as sperm and muscle, have many mitochondria with many cristae?
options: More cristae provide more surface for the ETC and ATP synthase, producing more ATP.
items.answer: More cristae provide more surface for the ETC and ATP synthase, producing more ATP.
items.markingKey: A. Structure–function link.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Chloroplasts are found in all plant cells and produce all their ATP." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many plant cells (e.g. roots) lack chloroplasts; plant cells use mitochondria for respiratory ATP; chloroplast ATP is mainly used in the Calvin cycle.
items.markingKey: Many plant cells (e.g. roots) lack chloroplasts; plant cells use mitochondria for respiratory ATP; chloroplast ATP is mainly used in the Calvin cycle. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An electron micrograph of a mitochondrion at × 40 000 shows it as 60 mm long. What is its actual length?
items.answer: 1.5 µm

items.stem: Using flight muscle of hummingbirds as an example, explain the structure–function relationship of mitochondria.
items.answer: Mitochondria occupy about 35 % of muscle fibre volume and have very dense cristae. Extensive cristae maximise ATP production to power wingbeats of up to 80 per second.
items.markingKey: Context (Mitochondria occupy about 35 % of muscle fibre volume and have very dense cristae.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Extensive cristae maximise ATP production to power wingbeats of up to 80 per second. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the structure–function relationship of mitochondria.

items.stem: Compare the structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts and explain how each is adapted to its function.
items.answer: Both: double membrane, own DNA, 70S ribosomes, internal membranes with ATP synthase, proton gradients. Mitochondria: cristae, matrix (Krebs), small intermembrane space. Chloroplasts: thylakoids/grana with pigments, lumen, stroma (Calvin), starch grains. Adaptations explained.
items.markingKey: Both: double membrane, own DNA, 70S ribosomes, internal membranes with ATP synthase, proton gradients. Mitochondria: cristae, matrix (Krebs), small intermembrane space. Chloroplasts: thylakoids/grana with pigments, lumen, stroma (Calvin), starch grains. Adaptations explained.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "granum"?
options: An unspecialised cell that can divide repeatedly and differentiate into specialised cell types
The separation of organelles by homogenising cells and centrifuging at increasing speeds (differential centrifugation)
A stack of thylakoids in a chloroplast
A protein-lined opening in the nuclear envelope that controls movement of molecules such as mRNA between nucleus and cytoplasm
items.answer: A stack of thylakoids in a chloroplast
items.markingKey: C. "granum" is a stack of thylakoids in a chloroplast.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of the mitochondrion is adapted to its function.
items.answer: Double membrane: outer controls entry; inner folded into cristae with large surface area for ETC and ATP synthase; small intermembrane space allows a steep proton gradient; matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle; own DNA and ribosomes to make some proteins.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Double membrane: outer controls entry; inner folded into cristae with large surface area for ETC and ATP synthase; small intermembrane space allows a steep proton gradient; matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle; own DNA and ribosomes to make some proteins. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the matrix of a mitochondrion and the stroma of a chloroplast.
items.answer: The matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle; the stroma contains enzymes of the Calvin cycle; both are fluid compartments with DNA and 70S ribosomes.
items.markingKey: The matrix contains enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle; the stroma contains enzymes of the Calvin cycle; both are fluid compartments with DNA and 70S ribosomes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mitochondria from heart muscle have more densely packed cristae than those from liver. Which prediction follows?
options: Heart mitochondria have a higher rate of oxidative phosphorylation per mitochondrion.
Liver mitochondria make more ATP per mitochondrion.
items.answer: Heart mitochondria have a higher rate of oxidative phosphorylation per mitochondrion.
items.markingKey: B. More membrane area = more ATP synthase.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The structures of mitochondria and chloroplasts are adapted mainly for chemiosmosis."
items.answer: Chemiosmosis explains many shared features, but each organelle’s structure reflects several functions and its evolutionary history.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: both have membranes enclosing small spaces where proton gradients build up and ATP synthase is embedded; membrane folding/stacking maximises area for these proteins. Arguments against: other features (matrix and stroma enzymes, DNA, ribosomes) are adapted for other stages and for self-maintenance; their double membranes reflect endosymbiotic origin as well as function. Supported judgement: Chemiosmosis explains many shared features, but each organelle’s structure reflects several functions and its evolutionary history. items.answer: Chemiosmosis explains many shared features, but each organelle’s structure reflects several functions and its evolutionary history.

items.stem: What causes cells with the same genome to differentiate into different types?
options: different genes are expressed in different cells
items.answer: different genes are expressed in different cells
items.markingKey: A. Gene expression determines cell type.

items.stem: Why can induced pluripotent stem cells reduce ethical concerns?
options: They are made from adult body cells, so no embryo is destroyed.
items.answer: They are made from adult body cells, so no embryo is destroyed.
items.markingKey: A. Reprogramming adult cells.

items.stem: Explain the difference between multipotent stem cells and pluripotent stem cells.
items.answer: Pluripotent cells can form any body cell type; multipotent cells can only form a limited range of related types, e.g. blood cells from bone marrow stem cells.
items.markingKey: Pluripotent cells can form any body cell type; multipotent cells can only form a limited range of related types, e.g. blood cells from bone marrow stem cells. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Specialised cells contain only the genes they need." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Specialised cells contain the full genome; they differ in which genes are expressed.
items.markingKey: Specialised cells contain the full genome; they differ in which genes are expressed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A patient’s own skin cells are reprogrammed into iPS cells and differentiated into retinal cells to treat macular degeneration. What is a key advantage?
options: The cells are genetically identical to the patient, so rejection is avoided.
The cells can never become cancerous.
items.answer: The cells are genetically identical to the patient, so rejection is avoided.
items.markingKey: C. Autologous cells match the immune system.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The use of embryonic stem cells in research is ethically justified."
items.answer: Many societies permit regulated research on surplus embryos for serious medical aims; the availability of iPS cells weakens but does not eliminate the case.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: potential to treat serious diseases such as Parkinson’s and diabetes; surplus IVF embryos would otherwise be discarded. Arguments against: destruction of embryos that some consider to have moral status; iPS cells offer alternatives without embryo destruction. Supported judgement: Many societies permit regulated research on surplus embryos for serious medical aims; the availability of iPS cells weakens but does not eliminate the case.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "totipotent".
items.answer: Describes a stem cell able to differentiate into any cell type, including extra-embryonic tissues (e.g. the zygote)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: describes a stem cell able to differentiate into any cell type, including extra-embryonic tissues (e.g. the zygote). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how differentiation results from gene expression.
items.answer: All body cells contain the same genes; during differentiation specific genes are switched on (transcribed) and others off, so each cell type makes particular proteins that give it its structure and function; patterns are controlled by signals and transcription factors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: All body cells contain the same genes; during differentiation specific genes are switched on (transcribed) and others off, so each cell type makes particular proteins that give it its structure and function; patterns are controlled by signals and transcription factors. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Shinya Yamanaka’s production of induced pluripotent stem cells (2006), explain how it illustrates gene expression in differentiation.
items.answer: Four transcription factors reprogrammed adult mouse skin cells into pluripotent cells. Switching on specific genes reversed differentiation, showing cell identity depends on gene expression.
items.markingKey: Context (Four transcription factors reprogrammed adult mouse skin cells into pluripotent cells.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Switching on specific genes reversed differentiation, showing cell identity depends on gene expression. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gene expression in differentiation.

items.stem: "Specialised cells contain only the genes they need." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Specialised cells contain the full genome; they differ in which genes are expressed.
items.markingKey: Specialised cells contain the full genome; they differ in which genes are expressed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the properties and types of stem cells and discuss their therapeutic uses.
items.answer: Self-renewal, differentiation; totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent; niches (bone marrow, hair follicle); differentiation by gene expression; uses: bone marrow transplants, skin grafts, research on iPS-derived cells; issues: ethics of embryos, rejection, tumour risk.
items.markingKey: Self-renewal, differentiation; totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent; niches (bone marrow, hair follicle); differentiation by gene expression; uses: bone marrow transplants, skin grafts, research on iPS-derived cells; issues: ethics of embryos, rejection, tumour risk.

items.stem: Why do sperm cells contain many mitochondria in their midpiece?
options: to supply ATP for the movement of the flagellum
to store food for the embryo
items.answer: to supply ATP for the movement of the flagellum
items.markingKey: A. Swimming requires much ATP.

items.stem: Distinguish between a sperm cell and an egg cell.
items.answer: Sperm are small, mobile, with a flagellum, mitochondria and acrosome; eggs are large, non-motile, rich in cytoplasm and nutrients with protective layers; both are haploid.
items.markingKey: Sperm are small, mobile, with a flagellum, mitochondria and acrosome; eggs are large, non-motile, rich in cytoplasm and nutrients with protective layers; both are haploid. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does a low SA:V ratio limit cell size?
options: Exchange across the surface becomes too slow to supply the larger volume’s metabolic needs.
items.answer: Exchange across the surface becomes too slow to supply the larger volume’s metabolic needs.
items.markingKey: C. Rate of exchange ∝ area; demand ∝ volume.

items.stem: Agar cubes of side 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm containing indicator are placed in acid. Which cube becomes completely coloured first, and why?
options: the 1 cm cube, because it has the highest SA:V ratio and shortest distance to the centre
the 3 cm cube, because it has the largest surface area
items.answer: the 1 cm cube, because it has the highest SA:V ratio and shortest distance to the centre
items.markingKey: A. SA:V 6, 3 and 2 cm⁻¹.

items.stem: A flattened cell is modelled as a cuboid 8 µm × 8 µm × 1 µm. Calculate its SA:V ratio and compare it with a cube of the same volume (side 4.0 µm). Explain the advantage of the flattened shape.
items.answer: cuboid 2.50 µm⁻¹; cube 1.50 µm⁻¹; flattening increases SA:V and reduces diffusion distance
items.markingKey: Cuboid SA = 160 µm², V = 64 µm³, ratio 2.50 (A1); cube ratio 6/4.0 = 1.50 (A1); higher SA:V / shorter distance to centre (R1).

items.stem: Using red blood cells as an example, explain the relationship between cell shape, SA:V and function.
items.answer: Mammalian erythrocytes are biconcave discs about 7.5 µm across and lack a nucleus. The biconcave shape increases SA:V for rapid O₂ diffusion and lack of nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin.
items.markingKey: Context (Mammalian erythrocytes are biconcave discs about 7.5 µm across and lack a nucleus.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The biconcave shape increases SA:V for rapid O₂ diffusion and lack of nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the relationship between cell shape, SA:V and function.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Surface area-to-volume ratio is the main factor limiting cell size."
items.answer: SA:V is a major constraint, but nuclear control and transport mechanisms also matter; exceptions show how cells adapt around the limit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diffusion rates depend on surface area while demand depends on volume; large cells (e.g. neurones, muscle fibres, eggs) have shapes or features that offset low SA:V. Arguments against: the ability of one nucleus to control a large volume of cytoplasm also limits size; cytoplasmic streaming and active transport can partly overcome diffusion limits. Supported judgement: SA:V is a major constraint, but nuclear control and transport mechanisms also matter; exceptions show how cells adapt around the limit.

items.stem: Explain how SA:V ratio limits cell size and describe how the structures of three named specialised cells are adapted to their functions.
items.answer: SA:V falls with size; exchange vs demand; diffusion distance. Examples: red blood cell (biconcave, no nucleus), type I pneumocyte (thin), type II (surfactant), sperm (flagellum, mitochondria, acrosome), egg (large, nutrients), striated muscle (multinucleate, sarcomeres), cardiac muscle (branched, intercalated discs).
items.markingKey: SA:V falls with size; exchange vs demand; diffusion distance. Examples: red blood cell (biconcave, no nucleus), type I pneumocyte (thin), type II (surfactant), sperm (flagellum, mitochondria, acrosome), egg (large, nutrients), striated muscle (multinucleate, sarcomeres), cardiac muscle (branched, intercalated discs).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption"?
items.answer: microvilli
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of microvilli.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of type I and type II pneumocytes is related to their functions.
items.answer: Type I: extremely thin, flattened, cover most of the alveolar surface, minimising diffusion distance for gas exchange; type II: cuboidal, with many lamellar bodies that secrete surfactant, reducing surface tension so alveoli do not collapse.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Type I: extremely thin, flattened, cover most of the alveolar surface, minimising diffusion distance for gas exchange; type II: cuboidal, with many lamellar bodies that secrete surfactant, reducing surface tension so alveoli do not collapse. items.stem: "Muscle fibres are typical cells with one nucleus each." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Striated muscle fibres are multinucleate, formed by fusion of many myoblasts.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "striated muscle fibre".
items.answer: A long multinucleate muscle cell with repeating sarcomeres, formed by fusion of many cells

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cell fractionation"?

The fluid inside the inner mitochondrial membrane containing enzymes of the link reaction and Krebs cycle, 70S ribosomes and DNA
The separation of organelles by homogenising cells and centrifuging at increasing speeds (differential centrifugation)

items.markingKey: Both are striated with sarcomeres; skeletal fibres are long, multinucleate and under voluntary control; cardiac muscle cells are shorter, branched, usually with one nucleus and connected by intercalated discs for coordinated contraction. items.stem: "Chloroplasts are found in all plant cells and produce all their ATP." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many plant cells (e.g. roots) lack chloroplasts; plant cells use mitochondria for respiratory ATP; chloroplast ATP is mainly used in the Calvin cycle.

items.stem: Briefly describe bone marrow transplants for leukaemia and explain what it reveals about the therapeutic use of stem cells.
items.answer: Haematopoietic stem cells from a matched donor repopulate the patient’s marrow after chemotherapy. Multipotent donor stem cells self-renew and differentiate into all blood cell types.

items.stem: Outline one way in which alveolar pneumocytes in human lungs shows cell specialisation.
items.answer: Type I cells (about 0.15 µm thick) cover about 95 % of alveolar surface; type II cells secrete surfactant. Thin type I cells minimise diffusion distance; type II cells prevent alveolar collapse.
items.markingKey: Context (Type I cells (about 0.15 µm thick) cover about 95 % of alveolar surface; type II cells secrete surfactant.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe pancreatic acinar cells secreting digestive enzymes and explain what it reveals about the secretory pathway and compartmentalisation.
items.answer: Radioactive amino acids traced by Palade appeared first in rough ER, then the Golgi, then secretory vesicles. The sequence of organelles shows how proteins are made, processed and packaged in separate compartments.

items.stem: Outline one way in which flight muscle of hummingbirds shows the structure–function relationship of mitochondria.
items.answer: Mitochondria occupy about 35 % of muscle fibre volume and have very dense cristae. Extensive cristae maximise ATP production to power wingbeats of up to 80 per second.
items.markingKey: Context (Mitochondria occupy about 35 % of muscle fibre volume and have very dense cristae.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using Shinya Yamanaka’s production of induced pluripotent stem cells (2006) as an example, explain gene expression in differentiation.
items.answer: Four transcription factors reprogrammed adult mouse skin cells into pluripotent cells. Switching on specific genes reversed differentiation, showing cell identity depends on gene expression.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Surface area-to-volume ratio is the main factor limiting cell size."
items.answer: SA:V is a major constraint, but nuclear control and transport mechanisms also matter; exceptions show how cells adapt around the limit.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diffusion rates depend on surface area while demand depends on volume; large cells (e.g. neurones, muscle fibres, eggs) have shapes or features that offset low SA:V. Arguments against: the ability of one nucleus to control a large volume of cytoplasm also limits size; cytoplasmic streaming and active transport can partly overcome diffusion limits. Supported judgement: SA:V is a major constraint, but nuclear control and transport mechanisms also matter; exceptions show how cells adapt around the limit.

items.stem: Explain how compartmentalisation within eukaryotic cells is related to the functions of named organelles.
items.answer: Nucleus: separates transcription/translation, mRNA processing; RER/ribosomes: protein synthesis for secretion; Golgi: modification and packaging; lysosomes: hydrolases at low pH, isolated; mitochondria: respiration, proton gradient across inner membrane; chloroplasts; vesicles; advantages: concentration, separation, gradients.
items.markingKey: Nucleus: separates transcription/translation, mRNA processing; RER/ribosomes: protein synthesis for secretion; Golgi: modification and packaging; lysosomes: hydrolases at low pH, isolated; mitochondria: respiration, proton gradient across inner membrane; chloroplasts; vesicles; advantages: concentration, separation, gradients.

items.stem: "The structures of mitochondria and chloroplasts are adapted mainly for chemiosmosis." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Chemiosmosis explains many shared features, but each organelle’s structure reflects several functions and its evolutionary history.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: both have membranes enclosing small spaces where proton gradients build up and ATP synthase is embedded; membrane folding/stacking maximises area for these proteins. Arguments against: other features (matrix and stroma enzymes, DNA, ribosomes) are adapted for other stages and for self-maintenance; their double membranes reflect endosymbiotic origin as well as function. Supported judgement: Chemiosmosis explains many shared features, but each organelle’s structure reflects several functions and its evolutionary history. items.stem: "The use of embryonic stem cells in research is ethically justified." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Many societies permit regulated research on surplus embryos for serious medical aims; the availability of iPS cells weakens but does not eliminate the case.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: potential to treat serious diseases such as Parkinson’s and diabetes; surplus IVF embryos would otherwise be discarded. Arguments against: destruction of embryos that some consider to have moral status; iPS cells offer alternatives without embryo destruction. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "type II pneumocyte"?
options: An alveolar cell that secretes surfactant to reduce surface tension
A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function
A flattened membrane sac in the chloroplast containing photosystems and ATP synthase, where light-dependent reactions occur
Describes a stem cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the body, but not the placenta (e.g. embryonic stem cells)
items.answer: An alveolar cell that secretes surfactant to reduce surface tension
items.markingKey: A. "type II pneumocyte" is an alveolar cell that secretes surfactant to reduce surface tension.

items.stem: Which feature increases the surface area for light absorption in chloroplasts?
items.answer: many thylakoids stacked into grana

items.stem: Why are embryonic stem cells potentially more useful in therapy than adult stem cells?
options: They are always genetically identical to the patient.
They are pluripotent and can form any body cell type.
items.answer: They are pluripotent and can form any body cell type.
items.markingKey: C. Adult stem cells are more limited.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of sperm and egg cells relates to their functions.
items.answer: Sperm: small, streamlined, flagellum for swimming, many mitochondria for ATP, acrosome with enzymes to penetrate the egg, haploid nucleus; egg: large with cytoplasm and nutrients for early development, zona pellucida and cortical granules to prevent polyspermy, haploid nucleus.

items.stem: Explain the properties of stem cells that make them useful in medicine.
items.answer: They can self-renew (divide repeatedly) and differentiate into specialised cells; so they can replace damaged tissues (e.g. bone marrow transplants, potential treatment of diabetes or Parkinson’s); pluripotent cells have the widest potential.

items.stem: "Prokaryotes are inefficient because they lack a nucleus." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Prokaryotes are highly successful; without a nucleus they can transcribe and translate simultaneously and respond rapidly, though they cannot process mRNA in the same way.

items.answer: Chloroplasts in shade leaves have larger grana with more thylakoids. More thylakoid membrane holds more light-harvesting pigment, capturing more of the limited light.

items.stem: "Compartmentalisation explains the success of eukaryotic cells." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Compartmentalisation enabled eukaryotic complexity, but “success” can also be measured by abundance and diversity, where prokaryotes excel.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it allows larger cells with specialised, efficient internal environments; it underpins multicellularity and complex regulation. Arguments against: prokaryotes are more numerous and metabolically diverse, and thrive without it; compartments add energy costs for transport between them. items.stem:
Cubes of agar containing phenolphthalein (pink in alkali) were placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The time taken for each cube to become completely colourless was recorded.

Side length / cm | SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹ | Time to decolourise / min
0.5 | 12.0 | 0.1
1.0 | 6.0 | 0.2
1.5 | ? | 0.3
2.0 | 3.0 | 0.4
2.5 | 2.4 | 0.5

(a) Calculate the SA:V ratio of the 1.5 cm cube. [2]
(b) Describe the relationship between SA:V ratio and the time taken to decolourise. [1]
(c) Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of acid into the 2.5 cm cube in cm per minute. [2]
(d) Explain why the larger cubes took longer to decolourise. [2]
items.answer: (a) 4.0 cm⁻¹ (b) As SA:V ratio decreases (larger cubes), time increases. (c) 2.500 cm min⁻¹ (d) They have a smaller SA:V ratio, so less surface for acid to enter per unit volume, and a greater distance from the surface to the centre.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] SA = 6 × 1.5² = 13.50; V = 3.375 (M1); ratio 4.0 (A1). (b) [1] Inverse relationship described (A1). (c) [2] Distance to centre = 1.25 cm (M1); 1.25/0.5 = 2.500 cm min⁻¹ (A1). (d) [2] Lower SA:V (A1); longer diffusion distance (A1).

items.stem:
Cubes of agar containing phenolphthalein (pink in alkali) were placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. The time taken for each cube to become completely colourless was recorded.

Side length / cm | SA:V ratio / cm⁻¹ | Time to decolourise / min
0.5 | 12.0 | 0.1
1.0 | 6.0 | 0.2
1.5 | 4.0 | 0.2
2.0 | ? | 0.3
2.5 | 2.4 | 0.4

(a) Calculate the SA:V ratio of the 2.0 cm cube. [2]
(b) Describe the relationship between SA:V ratio and the time taken to decolourise. [1]
(c) Calculate the mean rate of diffusion of acid into the 2.5 cm cube in cm per minute. [2]
(d) Explain why the larger cubes took longer to decolourise. [2]
(e) Relate these results to the size of cells. [2]
(f) Identify two sources of error and suggest improvements. [2]
(g) Suggest why the cubes were fully immersed and not touching the container. [1]
items.answer: (a) 3.0 cm⁻¹ (b) As SA:V ratio decreases (larger cubes), time increases. (c) 3.125 cm min⁻¹ (d) They have a smaller SA:V ratio, so less surface for acid to enter per unit volume, and a greater distance from the surface to the centre. (e) Cells must stay small (or flattened/folded) so that diffusion can supply the whole volume fast enough; large cells would have centres that receive materials too slowly. (f) Judging the colour end-point by eye – use a white tile/repeat; inaccurately cut cubes – use a template/measure with calipers; temperature/acid concentration variation – control. (g) So acid can diffuse in through all six faces and SA is as calculated.

(c) [2] Distance to centre = 1.25 cm (M1); 1.25/0.4 = 3.125 cm min⁻¹ (A1). (d) [2] Lower SA:V (A1); longer diffusion distance (A1). (e) [2] Diffusion too slow for large volumes (A1); cells divide/have adaptations to keep SA:V high (R1). (f) [2] Two errors with improvements (A1 A1). (g) [1] All faces exposed (A1).
